analysis.investment_thesis: JK Lakshmi Cement trades at INR 674 — roughly 74% above my calculated Graham Number of ~INR 387 (sqrt(22.5 × EPS₂₂.₂ × BVPS₂₉₉)) — offering no margin of safety whatsoever. Compounding the overvaluation, FY2025 net profit collapsed 43% YoY to INR 276 Cr while debt surged 28% to INR 2,673 Cr, precisely the combination of deteriorating earnings and rising leverage I find most dangerous.
key_strengths: Ten consecutive years of positive earnings (even if volatile), satisfying my minimum earnings continuity requirement
Operating cash flow positive all five recent years (INR 650–1,032 Cr), confirming the business generates real cash
Interest coverage ~5x (EBITDA INR 897 Cr ÷ Finance Cost INR 181 Cr), comfortably above my 3.5x floor
key_risks: Price far above Graham Number (~74% premium): no margin of safety at INR 674 vs calculated intrinsic value of ~INR 387
Debt/Equity of 0.72 exceeds my 0.50 limit; borrowings jumped from INR 2,084 Cr (FY24) to INR 2,673 Cr (FY25) — a 28% surge in one year
Earnings power severely deteriorating: net profit fell 43% in FY2025 to INR 276 Cr and FCF was negative in both FY2023 (−INR 98 Cr) and FY2024 (−INR 107 Cr)
red_flags: P/B of 2.26 — well above my hard limit of 1.5; I am paying INR 2.26 for every INR 1 of net assets in a commodity business
P/E of 17.5 on already-depressed FY2025 earnings; on normalized earnings the multiple is even worse
Revenue contracted in FY2025 (INR 6,193 Cr vs INR 6,788 Cr in FY2024) — top-line reversal in a capex-heavy cycle is alarming
Cash position of only INR 76 Cr against INR 2,673 Cr in borrowings — razor-thin liquidity buffer
EBITDA trend contracting (INR 1,109 Cr FY24 → INR 897 Cr FY25) while capex remains heavy (INR 661 Cr in FY25)
analysis.detailed_analysis:
From my strictly quantitative standpoint, JK Lakshmi Cement fails almost every screen I apply. The Graham Number — my bedrock test — yields approximately INR 387 against a market price of INR 674, meaning the stock must fall 43% merely to reach fair value by my measure. The P/B of 2.26 and P/E of 17.5 both breach my maximum thresholds of 1.5 and 15 respectively. Debt-to-equity at 0.72 exceeds my 0.50 ceiling, and the acceleration of borrowings by INR 589 Cr in a single year while profits cratered is precisely the pattern that precedes financial distress in commodity businesses. The cement industry is inherently cyclical with no durable pricing power — the sort of business where Mr. Market's optimism routinely leads the ordinary investor to overpay.

The one concession I grant this company is operational longevity: 86 years in business, a decade of unbroken (if lumpy) profitability, and consistent operating cash generation. However, the intelligent investor does not pay for history alone — the price must reflect an adequate discount to intrinsic value. With FCF negative in two of the last three years, a 43% profit collapse in FY2025, rising finance costs (INR 181 Cr in FY25 vs INR 150 Cr in FY24), and a cash reserve of only INR 76 Cr against over INR 2,600 Cr in debt, the balance sheet offers scant protection against further deterioration. I would require the price to fall to at least INR 350–400 — near or below the Graham Number — before any consideration of purchase.
